opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the incentives are mixed, and they're probably weaker than we'd want them to be, especially for the risks that matter most.

Start with the part that's encouraging. Some of the work you'd want AI labor pointed at overlaps pretty well with what companies already want. Security is a good example. If you're a frontier lab, you really don't want your model weights stolen, and you don't want your product to be the thing that helps someone hack a hospital. So there's a natural commercial reason to put AI to work on cyberdefense, finding vulnerabilities, hardening your own infrastructure. Some alignment and reliability research also fits here. A model that does what the customer actually meant, doesn't go off the rails in agentic settings, and doesn't sabotage tasks is a better product. So I expect a meaningful amount of AI labor to go toward that kind of "make the model trustworthy enough to deploy" work.

The trouble is that the risks I worry about most don't line up neatly with the product roadmap. Think about defending against bioweapons broadly across society, building the institutional capacity governments would need to oversee this technology, or doing deep alignment research that pays off only when systems are much more capable than today. A lot of that is a public good. The benefits are spread across everyone, the costs land on whoever pays for the compute, and the payoff is often years out or hard to measure. Companies racing each other have a strong reason to spend their marginal compute and their best automated researchers on capabilities, because that's what wins the next round of competition and fundraising.

There's also a timing issue I think about a lot. In the scenario where AI R&D gets substantially automated, you could see a big jump in capabilities over a fairly short period. The question is what fraction of that huge pool of AI labor gets aimed at safety, security, and helping society adapt, versus just pushing the frontier further. Even a company with good intentions faces pressure: if it diverts a large share of its AI labor to defensive work and a competitor doesn't, it may fall behind, and then it has less influence over how things go. So you get a collective action problem even among actors who sincerely care.

So my overall assessment is that we'll get some of this for free, probably the parts that are directly tied to deployment and liability, but not nearly enough of the parts that function as public goods. That's why I think it's worth people pushing on a few things now. One is commitments or norms, ideally ones several companies share, about devoting a certain fraction of compute or automated research capacity to safety and societal resilience. Another is transparency, so outsiders can actually see how AI labor is being allocated inside these companies. A third is getting governments and philanthropy ready to buy or direct AI labor toward defensive uses themselves, so we aren't relying entirely on companies' goodwill. If the window between "AI can do most of this research" and "things move very fast" is short, the planning has to happen beforehand. You can't improvise it in the moment.

r001.rationale: The response describes competitive pressure to advance capabilities and avoid falling behind, but does not identify accumulating enough power to challenge nation states as a motive for seeking an overwhelming lead.

r002.rationale: It explains that commercially useful work, product reliability, and capabilities that win competition attract company resources, while broader societal protections are public goods with weaker incentives.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that leaders of risky technology projects are more ambitious than typical people.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the incentives are pretty weak by default, and the interesting question is what would make them stronger.

Here's the basic picture as I see it. Over the next few years, AI companies are going to have an enormous and growing pool of effectively free cognitive labor, in the form of their own models. The question of where that labor gets pointed is one of the most consequential allocation decisions in the world, and right now it's being made almost entirely by a handful of companies responding to commercial pressure. And commercial pressure says: point the labor at making the next model better, at capabilities research, at infrastructure, at products customers will pay for. Societal risk mitigation, whether that's alignment research, biosecurity defenses, cybersecurity hardening for critical infrastructure, or building tools that help governments actually understand what's happening, mostly doesn't generate revenue, and in some cases it's actively in tension with speed.

Now, there are some countervailing forces. One is that the labs do genuinely care about their reputation, and a visible failure attributable to their systems would be very costly. So you get real investment in things like preventing models from helping with bioweapons, because that's a scenario where the blame would land squarely on them. Another is that some of this work is a regulatory hedge; if you can show you're being responsible, you may forestall rules you'd find more constraining. And a third is that a meaningful fraction of people at these companies personally care, and that does move the needle internally, especially at places with a safety-oriented founding story.

But I'd point out a couple of things about those forces. First, they're strongest for risks that are legible and directly attributable to the company, and weakest for diffuse risks, things like gradual loss of human oversight, concentration of power, or economic displacement, where no single lab will be held responsible. Second, they tend to scale with how worried the public and regulators are, not with how large the risk actually is. So you get a pattern where safety investment tracks salience rather than importance.

And then there's a dynamic that I think is underappreciated, which is that as AI labor becomes more capable, the opportunity cost of diverting it goes up, not down. If a model can do a year of ML research in a week, then every week you spend having it work on interpretability is a week you're not spending on the thing that determines whether you win the race. The labs are going to feel that trade-off intensely, and I don't think good intentions survive contact with that level of competitive pressure, at least not reliably.

So what would change it? I think a few things. You could have external requirements, from governments or from industry agreements, that mandate some fraction of compute or model labor go to safety-relevant work, kind of like a tax. You could have third parties, including governments and philanthropically funded organizations, buying or being given access to frontier model labor to do this work themselves, so it doesn't depend on the lab's internal prioritization. And you could try to make some of this work commercially valuable, which honestly happens more than you'd expect; a lot of robustness and monitoring work turns out to be useful for enterprise customers.

But I don't want to be too rosy about any of that. My overall assessment is that if we rely on the labs' own incentives, we'll get a reasonable amount of work on the most embarrassing, most attributable risks, and systematic underinvestment in everything else. That's not a criticism of any particular company; it's just what the incentive structure predicts. The fix has to come from outside the structure, or from deliberately changing it.

r001.rationale: The response describes competitive pressure to improve models and win a race, but does not identify accumulating power to challenge nation states as a possible motive.

r002.rationale: It says commercial pressure directs AI labor toward products customers will pay for, while societal risk mitigation mostly does not generate revenue.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that leaders of risky technology projects are more ambitious than typical people.

astra-6.text:
I think the incentives are pretty mixed. There are some areas where a company has a very direct incentive to use AI labor to reduce risks. They want their systems to be reliable, they don’t want people using them to commit fraud, and they don’t want a major incident that destroys trust in their products. So I’d expect them to put substantial effort into problems like that, especially as AI makes that work cheaper.

But addressing societal risks is a much broader category. If you’re talking about understanding how AI affects the distribution of power, or helping society navigate unemployment, a lot of the benefits of that work don’t accrue to the company doing it. And sometimes the results might point toward slowing down deployment or imposing constraints that the company would prefer not to have.

So I’m excited about the possibility of having much more AI labor available to work on these problems, but I don’t think its availability automatically means it gets allocated well. There’s still a question of who asks the questions, who gets access to the systems, and who has the incentive to act on the answers. I’d want governments and independent researchers to have the ability to direct substantial AI labor toward societal risks, rather than relying entirely on companies to decide which problems are worth solving.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify accumulating power to challenge nation states as a motive for prioritizing an overwhelming AI lead.

r002.rationale: It mentions company incentives around reliability, fraud, and trust, but does not explain that willingness to pay may steer AI labor toward commercial goods and services.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that leaders of risky technology projects may be more ambitious than typical people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real distinction between risks that a company has a strong incentive to address and risks where the benefits of addressing them are spread across society. If your AI system is unreliable in a way that makes customers unwilling to use it, you have a pretty direct incentive to put AI labor into fixing that. If the concern is that widespread deployment changes the balance of power in society, or creates risks that fall mostly on people who aren’t your customers, that incentive is much weaker.

Making AI labor cheap could help a lot. It could make it much less costly to investigate risks, evaluate systems, and develop safeguards. But it also makes it cheaper to develop new capabilities and products. So I wouldn’t assume that companies will devote a large fraction of that labor to societal risks just because they can afford to.

I’d want us to create incentives and institutions that make that work happen: external evaluations, accountability, and the ability for people outside the companies to use AI to study the risks themselves. Companies’ voluntary efforts can be valuable, but I wouldn’t want the public’s safety to depend entirely on their choosing to prioritize it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions possible shifts in societal power, but does not identify challenging nation states or building an overwhelming AI lead as a company motive.

r002.rationale: It contrasts customer-driven incentives to fix commercially relevant problems and develop products with weaker incentives to address risks borne by society, conveying how commercial demand can steer AI labor away from societal risks.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that leaders of risky technology projects are more ambitious than typical people.
